idiom_name: request-object decoration (req.user set by middleware) with AsyncLocalStorage for code off the request path
implementation_notes: The classic container collapses into the framework's request object: an authentication middleware verifies once and writes the principal onto the request (req.user, the Express/Passport convention), and every downstream route, guard and error handler reads the same object, so no context class is needed. When code runs without the request - a helper called from a queue consumer, a logger deep in a service - the Node runtime provides AsyncLocalStorage, documented as associating state with and propagating it through callbacks and promise chains (the closest equivalent to thread-local storage, with run() establishing a store for one asynchronous execution). What replaces the classic holder is therefore the request object on the normal path and one AsyncLocalStorage store on the ambient path; pick one as the canonical source and derive the other at the boundary instead of letting them diverge.
pitfalls: req.user is trustworthy only where the middleware ran: a route mounted before the authenticator sees undefined, so guards must fail closed rather than assume the property exists.

AsyncLocalStorage stores are bound to async resources: a callback created before run(), a detached resource or a native addon context sees no store, so snapshot()/bind() or explicit passing is needed across those hops.
Worker threads, child processes and message brokers do not inherit the store: the principal must be serialized and rebound at each boundary instead of assumed to travel.
